entries.meaning: To put a seed or a young plant into the ground so that it will grow. ---
examples: We plant tomatoes every year around Mother's Day.
They planted two hundred apple trees last spring.
The corn was planted too early and the frost killed it.

entries.meaning: To prepare and use land for growing crops, or to grow a particular crop. ---
examples: Farmers in this valley cultivate rice and beans.
His family cultivated the same hillside for a hundred years.
Only a third of the land is being cultivated now.

entries.meaning: To break up and turn over soil so that it is ready for planting. ---
examples: We till the garden as soon as the ground thaws.
He tilled four acres before breakfast.
The field has been tilled and is ready for seed.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the word till meaning 'until', but this one is a verb: till the soil.

entries.meaning: To turn over soil with a plow, or to push snow off a road. ---
examples: They plow the north field every fall.
He plowed the snow off the lane before dawn.
The ground has already been plowed twice.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (plow the north field), intransitive (they plowed until dark)
entries.contrast: American spelling is plow; British English writes plough. Same sound either way.

entries.meaning: To scatter seed over a piece of ground. ---
examples: We seed the lawn in early fall.
They seeded the pasture with clover.
The burned slope is being seeded by hand.

entries.meaning: To plant something again, or to plant new plants where old ones were. ---
examples: We replant the beds every spring.
They replanted the whole hillside after the fire.
Half the orchard has been replanted with younger trees.

entries.meaning: To add something to soil or plants to make them grow better. ---
examples: Fertilize the tomatoes once a month.
He fertilized the lawn in April.
The rows have been fertilized and watered.
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ize: fertilize, fertilized. British English writes fertilise.

entries.meaning: To cover soil with bark, straw, or leaves to hold in water and stop weeds. ---
examples: We mulch around the young trees every spring.
She mulched the flower beds with cedar bark.
The strawberry rows are mulched with straw.
entries.contrast: Third person takes -es after -ch: he mulches, not he mulchs.

entries.meaning: To bring water to dry land through pipes or ditches so crops can grow. ---
examples: They irrigate the fields with river water.
Settlers irrigated this whole valley by hand.
Nothing grows here unless the land is irrigated.

entries.meaning: To pour water on plants or give water to animals. ---
examples: Please water the tomatoes while we're away.
I watered the garden at sunrise.
The seedlings have not been watered in three days.
entries.contrast: No doubled t: watered, watering — the stress is on WAW-, so the t stays single.

entries.meaning: To pull wild plants out of a garden or field. ---
examples: I weed the beds every Saturday.
She weeded between the rows for two hours.
The path has been weeded and raked.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (weed the garden), intransitive (she weeded all morning)

entries.meaning: To break up soil or cut weeds with a hoe. ---
examples: They hoe the rows to keep the weeds down.
He hoed the bean patch after lunch.
She spent the whole morning hoeing.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hoe the bean rows), intransitive (he hoed until noon)
entries.contrast: Keeps its -e before -ing: hoeing, never hoing.

entries.meaning: To gather or smooth something with a rake. ---
examples: We rake the leaves every November.
He raked the gravel smooth.
The kids are raking the back yard.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rake the leaves), intransitive (we raked all afternoon)

entries.meaning: To move dirt, snow, or manure with a shovel. ---
examples: We shovel manure out of the barn every morning.
He shoveled the snow off the walk before school.
They have been shoveling since dawn.
entries.contrast: One l in American English: shoveled, shoveling. British English doubles it: shovelled.

entries.meaning: To cut branches off a tree or bush so it grows better. ---
examples: Prune the apple trees in late winter.
She pruned the roses back hard last month.
The grapevines have already been pruned.

entries.meaning: To join a branch of one plant onto another so they grow as one. ---
examples: Growers graft good fruit onto strong roots.
He grafted a pear branch onto the old tree.
These apples are grafted, not grown from seed.

entries.meaning: To support a plant by tying it to a wooden or metal stick. ---
examples: We stake the tomatoes as soon as they get tall.
He staked the young tree against the wind.
Every plant in that row has been staked.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like steak (the meat). Stake the tomatoes, grill the steak.

entries.meaning: To plant something in a pot rather than in the ground. ---
examples: I pot the herbs and keep them on the windowsill.
She potted the cuttings last week.
He is potting seedlings in the greenhouse.
entries.русский: сажать в горшок, пересаживать в горшок
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: pot → potted, potting.

entries.meaning: To grow new plants from seeds, cuttings, or runners. ---
examples: You can propagate mint from a single cutting.
She propagated dozens of tomatoes over the winter.
These shrubs are easily propagated in water.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (propagate mint from cuttings), intransitive (the plant propagates easily)

entries.meaning: To start to grow, especially for a seed sending up its first shoot. ---
examples: Radish seeds sprout in about four days.
The beans sprouted overnight.
New shoots are sprouting all along the fence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the tree sprouted new leaves), intransitive (the seeds sprouted)

entries.meaning: To begin to grow, said of a seed opening and putting out a root. ---
examples: These seeds germinate best in warm soil.
Only half the corn germinated that spring.
The seeds are germinating under the plastic.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the seeds germinate), transitive (germinate the seeds on a wet towel)

entries.meaning: To produce flowers. ---
examples: Our lilacs bloom in the middle of May.
The cactus bloomed for one single night.
The whole meadow is blooming after the rain.

entries.meaning: To open into flowers, especially on a fruit tree. ---
examples: Cherry trees blossom early here.
The orchard blossomed two weeks late this year.
The pear tree has finally blossomed.

entries.meaning: To form small swellings that will open into leaves or flowers. ---
examples: The maples bud before the oaks do.
The roses budded in early April.
The trees are budding along the river.
entries.contrast: Doubles the d: bud → budded, budding.

entries.meaning: To produce flowers. ---
examples: This plant flowers twice in a season.
The tomatoes flowered in early June.
The desert is flowering after a wet winter.

entries.meaning: To become fully grown or fully ripe. ---
examples: This corn matures in about ninety days.
The calves matured faster on the new feed.
The fruit is still maturing on the branch.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the cheese is matured in a cave), intransitive (the corn matures in ninety days)

entries.meaning: To grow strongly and healthily. ---
examples: Tomatoes flourish in this sandy soil.
The herd flourished after the wet spring.
The garden has flourished since we added compost.

entries.meaning: To grow roots and take hold in the soil. ---
examples: Willow cuttings root in plain water.
The transplants rooted within a week.
Half the cuttings have already rooted.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (root a cutting in water), intransitive (the cuttings rooted)
entries.contrast: Different from root for (= to support a team), which is a phrasal verb.

entries.meaning: To carry pollen to a flower so that it can produce fruit or seed. ---
examples: Bees pollinate almost the whole orchard.
Wind pollinated the corn in a single afternoon.
The blossoms have not been pollinated yet.

entries.meaning: To increase greatly in number, especially by breeding. ---
examples: Rabbits multiply faster than anyone expects.
The aphids multiplied in a single week.
The herd has multiplied since the drought ended.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (rabbits multiply fast), transitive (multiply the seed by hand)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie: multiplies, multiplied — but multiplying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To pull a plant out of the ground with its roots. ---
examples: Storms uproot the shallowest trees first.
The wind uprooted two apple trees last night.
Half the hedge had been uprooted by morning.

entries.meaning: To take fruit, flowers, or vegetables off the plant by hand. ---
examples: We pick apples the last week of September.
She picked three quarts of blueberries before noon.
These beans are picked by hand.

entries.meaning: To move a group of animals together from one place to another. ---
examples: The dogs herd the sheep down off the ridge.
He herded the cows into the barn before the storm.
The goats are being herded into the pen.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like heard, the past of hear. He herded the cows; I heard the cows.

entries.meaning: To take milk from a cow, goat, or other animal. ---
examples: We milk the goats twice a day.
He milked forty cows before breakfast.
The cows have already been milked this morning.

entries.meaning: To come out of an egg, or to bring young out of eggs. ---
examples: These eggs hatch in twenty-one days.
Four chicks hatched overnight.
The last egg has not hatched yet.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the chicks hatched), transitive (the hen hatched six eggs)
entries.contrast: Third person takes -es after -ch: it hatches, not it hatchs.

entries.meaning: To keep eggs warm until the young are ready to come out. ---
examples: A hen incubates her eggs for about three weeks.
We incubated the duck eggs in the back shed.
The eggs are being incubated at ninety-nine degrees.

entries.meaning: To make a young animal stop drinking its mother's milk and start eating other food. ---
examples: Ranchers wean the calves at about six months.
We weaned the lambs early that dry year.
The puppies have already been weaned.
entries.русский: отнимать от матери, отлучать от вымени
entries.contrast: Wean an animal off or from its mother's milk — off and from are the usual prepositions.

entries.meaning: To feed an animal well so that it puts on weight before sale or slaughter. ---
examples: They fatten the hogs on corn all fall.
The steers fattened fast on the new pasture.
The geese are being fattened for the holidays.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fatten the hogs on corn), intransitive (the steers fattened quickly)

entries.meaning: To make a wild animal used to people and safe to handle. ---
examples: It takes months to tame a wild horse.
She tamed the barn cat with a can of tuna.
That fox has never been fully tamed.

entries.meaning: To turn a wild species into one that lives with and works for people. ---
examples: People domesticate very few wild species.
Humans domesticated the horse thousands of years ago.
Goats were domesticated before cattle were.

entries.meaning: To kill an animal and cut it up for meat. ---
examples: We butcher one hog every November.
He butchered the deer that same evening.
The lamb has already been butchered and wrapped.

entries.meaning: To brush and clean an animal's coat. ---
examples: She grooms the horses every morning.
He groomed the pony before the county fair.
The dogs are groomed twice a year.

entries.meaning: To look after plants or animals and give them what they need. ---
examples: He tends the whole orchard by himself.
She tended the sheep through a hard winter.
That garden has been carefully tended for years.
entries.contrast: You can tend the animals or tend to the animals. Do not mix it up with tend to do something, which means 'usually do'.

entries.meaning: To put a fence around a piece of land. ---
examples: We fence the garden to keep the deer out.
They fenced forty acres last summer.
The pasture is fenced on three sides.

entries.meaning: To care for something young or weak so that it grows strong. ---
examples: Good soil nurtures deep roots.
She nurtured the seedlings all winter under lights.
The orphaned calf was nurtured by hand.

entries.meaning: To put straps on a horse or other animal so it can pull something. ---
examples: They still harness mules for the steepest rows.
He harnessed the team before sunrise.
The horses are already harnessed and waiting.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ss: he harnesses the team.

entries.meaning: To put a saddle on a horse. ---
examples: We saddle the horses right after chores.
She saddled her mare and rode out to the herd.
The ponies were saddled and ready by six.

entries.meaning: To come together with another animal to produce young. ---
examples: Geese mate for life.
The pair mated in early spring.
Several of the foxes are mating this month.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (geese mate for life), transitive (they mated the mare with a local stallion)
entries.contrast: Animals mate with each other: the female mates with one male only.

entries.meaning: To build a nest and live in it while raising young. ---
examples: Swallows nest under our barn roof every year.
A pair of owls nested in the old sycamore.
The turtles are nesting on the beach tonight.

entries.meaning: To settle somewhere high for the night, said of birds. ---
examples: The hens roost up in the rafters.
Hundreds of crows roosted in the bare trees.
The chickens were already roosting when we got home.

entries.meaning: To sit on a branch, wire, or post, said of a bird. ---
examples: Hawks perch on the fence posts along this road.
A cardinal perched on the feeder for a second.
Two owls were perching on the barn ridge.

entries.meaning: To move or gather in a large crowd, said of bees and other insects. ---
examples: Bees swarm when the hive gets too crowded.
Mosquitoes swarmed around the pond all evening.
Locusts have been swarming across the valley.

entries.meaning: To sleep through the winter, said of animals like bears and groundhogs. ---
examples: Groundhogs hibernate from October to March.
The bear hibernated in a hollow log.
The frogs are hibernating down in the mud.

entries.meaning: To dig a hole or tunnel in the ground to live in. ---
examples: Rabbits burrow right under the garden fence.
A mole burrowed across the whole lawn.
Something has been burrowing in the carrot bed.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (rabbits burrow under the fence), transitive (it burrowed a tunnel)

entries.meaning: To lay eggs in water, said of fish and frogs. ---
examples: Salmon spawn in the stream where they hatched.
The trout spawned early this year.
Thousands of fish are spawning in the shallows.

entries.meaning: To lose old feathers, hair, or skin so that new ones can grow. ---
examples: Our hens molt every fall and stop laying.
The snake molted behind the woodpile.
The ducks are molting and look terrible.
entries.contrast: American spelling is molt; British English writes moult.

entries.meaning: To gather or travel in a large group, said especially of birds. ---
examples: Starlings flock to the field right after harvest.
The geese flocked to the one patch of open water.
Birds have been flocking to the feeder all morning.
entries.contrast: Birds flock to a place — the preposition is to.

entries.meaning: To go around searching for food in the wild. ---
examples: Deer forage at the edge of the woods at dusk.
The bears foraged along the creek all fall.
The chickens are foraging in the tall grass.
entries.contrast: Forage for something: the bears forage for berries.

entries.meaning: To hunt and eat another animal. ---
examples: Owls prey on mice and voles.
Coyotes preyed on the flock all spring.
Something has been preying on our chickens.
entries.contrast: Always prey on something. It sounds exactly like pray (to pray in church).

entries.meaning: To feed on dead animals or on food that others have left. ---
examples: Vultures scavenge whatever the coyotes leave.
The gulls scavenged along the shoreline.
Raccoons have been scavenging in the feed shed.
entries.русский: питаться падалью; рыться в поисках еды
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (vultures scavenge), transitive (they scavenged whatever was left)

entries.meaning: To strike or pick up something with the beak. ---
examples: The hens peck at the corn all day long.
A rooster pecked my ankle when I opened the gate.
The chicks are pecking their way out of the shells.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a rooster pecked my ankle), intransitive (the hens peck at the corn)
entries.contrast: Peck at something means to take small pecks at it: the birds peck at the seed.

entries.meaning: To fly or move with quick, light, irregular motions. ---
examples: Butterflies flutter over the clover all afternoon.
A moth fluttered against the lantern.
Leaves were fluttering down across the road.

entries.meaning: To move a tail quickly from side to side. ---
examples: Our dogs wag their tails at every truck that passes.
The puppy wagged its whole body, not just its tail.
He came running with his tail wagging.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: wag → wagged, wagging.

entries.meaning: To move along the ground with a smooth twisting motion, the way a snake does. ---
examples: Snakes slither right through the tall grass.
A garter snake slithered across the path.
Something was slithering under the porch.

entries.meaning: To run quickly with short light steps, the way a small animal does. ---
examples: Squirrels scamper along the fence rail all day.
A chipmunk scampered into the woodpile.
Mice were scampering through the hay.

entries.meaning: To lie in a warm place, especially in the sun, and enjoy the heat. ---
examples: Turtles bask on the logs every afternoon.
The lizard basked on a warm rock by the wall.
Two snakes were basking in the sun on the path.
entries.contrast: Bask in the sun — the preposition is in, not on.

entries.meaning: To move around quietly looking for something to catch. ---
examples: Coyotes prowl the fence line after dark.
A bobcat prowled around the henhouse last week.
Something has been prowling near the lambing pen.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the cat prowls the barn), intransitive (coyotes prowl at night)

entries.meaning: To jump suddenly onto something in order to catch it. ---
examples: Barn cats pounce the moment the grass moves.
The fox pounced on a mouse in the snow.
The hawk was pouncing on something out in the field.
entries.contrast: Pounce on something — the preposition is on.

entries.meaning: To fly down suddenly and steeply. ---
examples: Swallows swoop low over the mown field.
An eagle swooped down and took a fish.
A hawk is swooping toward the chicken yard.

entries.meaning: To make a short high sound, said of small birds and insects. ---
examples: Crickets chirp faster when the night is warm.
The chicks chirped in the box all night.
Sparrows were chirping in the hedge at dawn.

entries.meaning: To make a long loud crying sound, said of dogs, wolves, or the wind. ---
examples: Coyotes howl behind the barn most nights.
The dog howled until we let him in.
Wolves have been howling all along the ridge.

entries.meaning: To make the short loud sound a dog makes. ---
examples: Our dogs bark at every truck on the road.
The collie barked at the coyote until it left.
Something is barking down by the creek.
entries.contrast: The noun bark also means the outer skin of a tree — same spelling, different word.

entries.meaning: To make a low threatening sound in the throat, said of an animal. ---
examples: The old dog growls at anyone he doesn't know.
The bear growled once and backed away.
The pup was growling at his own reflection.

entries.meaning: To make a low steady sound of contentment, said of a cat. ---
examples: The barn cats purr the second you feed them.
The kitten purred on my lap for an hour.
She was already purring before I sat down.

entries.meaning: To make the long low call of an owl. ---
examples: Owls hoot from the tree line after dark.
An owl hooted twice and then went quiet.
Something has been hooting out there all night.

entries.meaning: To make the deep rough sound of a frog or a crow. ---
examples: Frogs croak along the pond every evening.
A bullfrog croaked right under the dock.
The tree frogs were croaking after the rain.

entries.meaning: To make the short repeated sound of a hen. ---
examples: The hens cluck whenever they see the feed bucket.
A hen clucked at her chicks to follow her.
The chickens are clucking out in the run.

entries.meaning: To make the sound a duck makes. ---
examples: The ducks quack the second you open the gate.
The ducklings quacked the whole way to the pond.
Something was quacking out in the reeds.

entries.meaning: To make a loud sharp high cry. ---
examples: Barn owls screech instead of hooting.
A hawk screeched over the pasture.
The peacocks have been screeching since dawn.
entries.contrast: Third person takes -es after -ch: it screeches.

entries.meaning: To run at the fastest pace, said of a horse. ---
examples: The horses gallop to the gate at feeding time.
She galloped across the open field.
A colt was galloping along the fence line.
entries.contrast: One p: galloped, galloping. The stress falls on GAL-, so the last consonant is not doubled.

entries.meaning: To move at a steady pace between walking and running, said of a horse. ---
examples: The ponies trot over as soon as they hear the bucket.
The mare trotted right up to the fence.
The colt was trotting beside its mother.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: trot → trotted, trotting.

entries.meaning: To chase and kill wild animals for food or sport. ---
examples: They hunt deer on that ridge every November.
His father hunted elk in Montana for thirty years.
Wolves have been hunting the herd all winter.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hunt deer), intransitive (they hunt every November)
entries.contrast: Hunt an animal, but hunt for something you have lost: I hunted for my keys.

entries.meaning: To try to catch fish. ---
examples: We fish the creek every spring.
They fished from the bank until it got dark.
He has been fishing since sunrise.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -sh: he fishes. You fish for trout — the preposition is for.

entries.meaning: To fall as water from the clouds. ---
examples: It rains almost every afternoon in July.
It rained on the cut hay for three days straight.
It has been raining since Tuesday.
entries.contrast: The subject is always it: It rained hard. Sounds like reign (of a king) and rein (of a horse).

entries.meaning: To fall as snow from the sky. ---
examples: It snows here from November to April.
It snowed six inches the night the calves came.
It was snowing hard when we finally got the herd in.
entries.contrast: Like rain, it takes it as its subject: It snowed all night.

entries.meaning: To make something completely wet. ---
examples: Summer storms drench these fields in minutes.
The rain drenched us before we reached the barn.
The pasture was drenched and too soft to drive on.

entries.meaning: To flow slowly through small openings in soil or a wall. ---
examples: Water seeps out of this hillside all year.
The rain seeped down to the roots overnight.
Fertilizer has been seeping into the creek.

entries.meaning: To flow in a thin, slow stream. ---
examples: A small spring trickles down over the rocks.
Water trickled out of the cracked pipe all day.
The creek was barely trickling by August.

entries.meaning: To turn from liquid into vapor and disappear into the air. ---
examples: Puddles evaporate fast in this heat.
Most of the water evaporated before it reached the roots.
The pond has been evaporating all summer.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the puddles evaporate), transitive (the sun evaporates the water)

entries.meaning: To block a stream or river so the water backs up behind a wall. ---
examples: Beavers dam this creek every single spring.
They dammed the stream to make a stock pond.
The river has been dammed since 1940.
entries.contrast: Doubles the m: dam → dammed, damming — which then looks like damn, a different word entirely.

entries.meaning: To make water or traffic go a different way. ---
examples: Growers divert river water into the orchards.
They diverted the creek around the new field.
The stream has been diverted twice in ten years.
entries.русский: отводить, отвести (воду); направлять в другую сторону

entries.meaning: To fill a place in large harmful numbers, said of insects or pests. ---
examples: Beetles infest the corn every August.
Aphids infested the whole greenhouse in a week.
The old barn is infested with mice.
entries.contrast: Usually passive: the field is infested with weevils — the preposition is with.

entries.meaning: To hide something by making it look like what is around it. ---
examples: Brown feathers camouflage the hen on her nest.
The moth camouflaged itself against the bark.
The nest was camouflaged with moss and grass.
entries.contrast: Spelling trap: -mou- in the middle and -flage at the end, but it ends in the sound -flahzh.

entries.meaning: To use land to grow crops or raise animals. ---
examples: They farm four hundred acres of wheat.
His family farmed this land for sixty years.
The valley has been farmed since the 1800s.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (farm four hundred acres), intransitive (they farm for a living)

entries.meaning: To work in a garden growing flowers or vegetables. ---
examples: My parents garden every weekend from April on.
She gardened well into her eighties.
He has been gardening since the snow melted.

entries.meaning: To cut down a tree. ---
examples: The crew fells the dead pines first.
They felled the old oak in under an hour.
Thousands of trees have been felled on this slope.
entries.contrast: Not the same as fell, the past of fall. The tree fell on its own; the crew felled the tree.

entries.meaning: To run in a sudden panic, said of a herd of animals. ---
examples: Cattle stampede at the first crack of thunder.
The herd stampeded straight through the fence.
The horses were stampeding toward the river.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the cattle stampeded), transitive (the thunder stampeded the herd)

entries.meaning: To burn a mark into an animal's hide to show who owns it. ---
examples: Ranchers brand the calves every spring.
They branded two hundred head that weekend.
Every steer here is branded on the left hip.

entries.meaning: To push or rub gently with the nose or mouth. ---
examples: The foals nuzzle your pockets looking for treats.
The calf nuzzled its mother and started to feed.
The horse was nuzzling my shoulder the whole time.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the calf nuzzled its mother), intransitive (the horse nuzzled at my hand)

entries.meaning: To scrape or touch something with a foot or hoof. ---
examples: Horses paw the ground when they get impatient.
The dog pawed at the barn door until we opened it.
A mare was pawing through the snow for grass.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the horse pawed the ground), intransitive (the dog pawed at the door)
entries.contrast: Paw at something when the animal keeps touching it: the cat paws at the window.

entries.meaning: To roll around in mud or water, said of animals. ---
examples: Hogs wallow in the mud to stay cool.
The buffalo wallowed in a dust hole all afternoon.
Two pigs were wallowing by the fence.

entries.meaning: To move in small waves across a surface. ---
examples: The wheat ripples whenever the wind crosses the field.
The pond rippled where a fish came up.
The tall grass was rippling like water.

entries.meaning: To improve a piece of ground by planting and shaping it. ---
examples: They landscape yards for a living.
We landscaped the slope with native grasses.
The whole property has been landscaped.

entries.meaning: To pull out some young plants so the rest have room to grow.
examples: Thin the carrots once they are two inches tall.
We thinned the apples so the rest would grow bigger.
The lettuce has been thinned twice already.
entries.contrast: Doubles the n: thin → thinned, thinning.
